title: Part 2.III — Act: Aristotle and Aquinas
role_in_volume: Third Part-2 chapter and the volume's STRONGEST EXEGETICAL anchor to existing corpus indices. Act is the pentad term Burke assigns to scholastic realism as its featured locus of motive: action-as-actualization (Aristotelian energeia as the bringing-out of dynamis into actuality) is the originating ground that explains both agent and scene. Burke reads Aristotle and Aquinas in tandem (the opening subsection is titled 'Aristotle and Aquinas') in five pages of densely packed primary-text exegesis covering Aristotle's four causes (Metaphysics + Physics), the energeia/dynamis pair, the entelechy, Poetics on tragedy-as-action, and Aquinas's commentaries (specifically Summa Contra Gentiles and the Aristotle commentaries in Everyman's Library). The chapter then develops four further apparatuses: (i) the 'pathetic fallacy' (motion-action ambiguity as the watershed dividing dramatistic from operationalist vocabularies); (ii) the 'incipient and delayed' act (Richards' incipient-action + Mead's attitudes-as-beginnings-of-acts + Korzybski's delayed-response — Burke's closest approach to a phenomenology of intention and the chapter's signature concept for cognitive-science crosswalks); (iii) realist family vs nominalist aggregate (the act-genus-generation tie-up); (iv) further remarks on act and potency (Aristotle's actuality-prior-to-potentiality, entelechy, ratio-as-potential-to-actual formula, Heisenberg digression). The closing 'Psychology of Action' subsection re-maps the entire chapter onto action-passion / actus-status / action-motion / potential pairs and runs them through Stoicism, Christian martyrdom, Eliot's Murder in the Cathedral, Hegelian Spirit, Rousseau, and Indo-European middle-voice grammar. This is the chapter that directly anchors Aristotle Complete Works + Phantasia Cluster + Bowin AMT + Heidegger BCAP cross-pipeline edges; every other Heidegger/Aristotle bridge in the pipeline runs through this chapter's Burke-Aristotle primary engagement.

outline.title: Aristotle and Aquinas (chapter-opening subsection — five pages of densest Aristotelian exegesis in the volume)
outline.summary: Burke opens with a Baldwin-dictionary citation chain establishing why realism features Act: 'In Aristotle things are more or less real according as they are more or less energeia (actu)' (p.227); in scholastic realism 'form is the actus, the attainment, which realizes the matter'; quoting Aquinas: 'forma per se ipsam facit rem esse in actu' (a form is an act); existence is 'the act of essence'; the soul is the 'act of an organic physical body capable of life'; Gilson on existence as 'an act, not a thing' (footnote on the copulative verb being grammatically active — sociologically wired to feudal status-maintenance); Aquinas on the agent-act ratio in Summa Contra Gentiles: 'every thing acts according as it is in act.' Burke then runs Aristotle's four causes through the pentad (pp.228-229 — the chapter's PENTAD-AS-FOUR-CAUSES MAPPING): material cause = Scene; efficient cause = Agent; final cause = Purpose; formal cause = Act; agency is incidental in Aristotle (subsumed under final cause, via Organon-as-instrument); Aquinas' Ibn-Sina four-fold efficient-cause expansion produces the 'auxiliary' or 'secondary' efficient cause = agent/agency overlap (co-agent vocabulary). Burke offers a NEGATIVE-WAY confirmation via the scholastic hexameter (quis, quid, ubi, quibus auxiliis, cur, quo modo, quando): quis=Agent, ubi+quando=Scene, cur=Purpose, quibus auxiliis+quo modo=Agency — only quid is left for Act, and the form of a thing was called quidditas ('whatness'). Brief observation that scholastic vocabulary is essentially dramatic but not consciously so — the direction was scientist, moving from act of faith to conditions of knowledge; the dramatism lay in the point of departure (Homeric epics, Dionysian dramas, drama of salvation, Socrates' Reality as 'power to act and to be acted upon'). The Aristotle-on-tragedy block (pp.230-231) supplies the chapter's Poetics anchor: 'Tragedy is essentially an imitation not of persons but of action and life' — Burke aligns Aristotle's six elements with his five pentad terms (plot=Act; character=Agent; thought=Purpose; melody+diction=Agency; spectacle=Scene-as-scenic-agency). Closing paragraph (p.231): Aristotle 'neutralized' Platonist realism by denying Ideas and God any generative function — Aristotelian teleology has each kind of thing striving to be perfectly the kind of thing it is (the entelechy seed), which 'allowed for much purely inductive study of genera and species' and made Aristotelian terminology adoptable by Aquinas as 'rationalizer of the Christian drama.'

outline.title: The 'Pathetic Fallacy' (motion-action ambiguity; Josephine Miles; scene-agent vs scene-act ratio; the watershed-moment dividing dramatism from operationalism)
outline.summary: Pivots from Aristotelian exegesis to the chapter's first methodological apparatus. Aristotle himself (Metaphysics IX) admits that energeia 'is thought to be identical with movement' though it has 'in the main been extended from movements to other things' — Burke notes the Greek roots (ergon = work/deed; pragma = thing-to-be-accomplished; chrema = thing-to-be-used; viewed pentadically 'pragmatism' might better be 'chrematism'). Josephine Miles's Pathetic Fallacy in the Nineteenth Century (Ruskin's term, attribution of human emotions to non-human objects: 'the trees were gay, the mountains mourned') is reinterpreted: Miss Miles's restricted definition tracks the scene-agent (or LYRIC) ratio, because the device attributes personal feelings (properties of agents) to scene. Burke EXTENDS the term to cover the broader 'action-motion ambiguity' (motion-personalization-as-act): 'the wheat tossed in the wind' is motion; 'the wheat tossed its head in the wind' is action. Coleridge on Venus and Adonis ('Look how a bright star shooteth from the sky') as imagination-via-empathy: do shooting stars move or act? Theory of empathy = we attribute action when we move with them imaginatively. Eliot's 'yellow smoke that slides along the street,' 'windings of the violins,' 'light that crept up between the shutters' — indebted to action-motion ambiguity for their force as Aristotelian 'actualizations.' Critical move: action-motion is the WATERSHED moment dividing dramatist from operationalist vocabularies (p.234). The realm of motion is now par excellence the realm of instruments — no instrument can record action ('ideas') except insofar as the subject-matter is reduced to motion. Cartesian dualism reappears: naturalist philosophers drawing 'doctrinal sustenance from unrecognized effects of the pathetic fallacy as we have here extended it.' Burke flags an 'active or policy-making function' integral to vocabularies of motivation — necessarily 'nonsense' as tested by technological vocabularies but realistic when arising out of tribal experience (proverbs); tending toward idealism in proportion as derived from managerial agents. Section closes by demanding 'fully worked-out version of the ways of homo dialecticus' rather than 'scraps of dialectical lore.'

outline.title: 'Incipient' and 'Delayed' Action (Richards' incipient act + Mead's attitudes-as-beginnings-of-acts + Korzybski's delayed response + Hamlet + the chapter's PHENOMENOLOGY-OF-INTENTION pivot)
outline.summary: Longest subsection (12 pp.) and the chapter's load-bearing CONCEPT-CLUSTER for cross-pipeline bridging. Opens with I. A. Richards (Principles of Literary Criticism, ch. on Attitudes): 'Every perception probably includes a response in the form of incipient action. We constantly overlook the extent to which all the while we are making preliminary adjustments, getting ready to act in one way or another' — the centipede-leaf example. Richards' analytic move: poetic response involves 'imaginal activities' and 'tendencies to action' — symbolic representation can arouse complex response because we feel emotions associated with the object/event while making allowance for the fiction; no overt action is called for, so the impulse stays incipient — Richards prizes this as intelligence/refinement (the 'stupid or crass person' habitually responds to impulses by overt action). Burke names the CHAPTER'S CENTRAL AMBIGUITY: the incipient act is double — an attitude can be SUBSTITUTE for an act OR FIRST STEP toward an act. Hence the rhetoric of advertisers and propagandists (who induce action via attitude-formation). Mead block (pp.236-238): Mind, Self, and Society — attitudes are 'the beginnings of acts'; The Philosophy of the Act could be re-titled The Philosophy of the Attitude. Mead distinguishes action from motion, but his action is internal-organism-confronting-resistance (analogous to Santayana's 'field of action'), giving 'action-minus' or 'attitude-minus.' The Meadian self emerges as the individual learns to take the 'attitude of the other' and to anticipate object-resistance ('the individual, in preparing to grasp the distant object, himself takes the attitude of resisting his own attitude in grasping') — Hegelian-dialectic pattern (Spirit alienated as Nature). Mead's social-self is complex of attitudes built atop biological motives, particularly modified by language as 'vocal gesture.' Korzybski block (pp.238-243): Science and Sanity. Korzybski offers a TECHNIQUE for encouraging 'delayed response' — not Richards' imagination-substitution but a wholesale rule that we delay every response because explanations are askew (Mead: 'overt or delayed response'). Burke: the sanity is personal-social-political, but the science is physics-physiology; Korzybski works better as a Rhetoric than a Grammar; his 'consciousness of abstracting' is a haphazardly rediscovered aspect of Neo-Platonism. Famous chair example (pp.240-241): consciously abstracting 'chair' as high-order classification, Korzybski sat down with 'usual attitude of delayed action'; the chair was frail, it collapsed, but the wary savant did not collapse with it — 'by participation in the Korzybski mathema, through the medium of a delayed poiema we may avoid a disconcerting pathema.' Footnote 8 (pp.239-240) sharpens: Korzybskian semantics is 'study of dialectic which is greatly truncated by reason of the fact that it did not formally and systematically recognize its dialectical nature.' Three-moment paradox (pp.241-242): physiological / mental / tertium-quid (body-mind / neuro-semantic) — Korzybski jumps between moments to evade refutation; reducing 'delayed action' to its physiological moment makes it the OPPOSITE of a delay (a state of delayed action cannot be a corresponding state of delayed motion; the body during delay does not cease to exist; the mental attitude of arrest must have its own physiological configuration). Burke's pivot back to Aristotle (pp.242-243): the attitude-as-incipient-act is 'a special application of the concept of POTENTIALITY,' which in Aristotle's dramatist Grammar was 'the reciprocal of actuality' (Metaphysics IX.8: 'Every potency is at one and the same time a potency of the opposite'); the hot is potentially the cold; matter is the realm of potentiality, hence in being potentially good matter is potentially bad. Latin inceptive/inchoative verb-forms (calesco / irascor) confirm the ambiguous-incipient territory. Realm of the incipient is the realm of SYMBOLIC ACTION par excellence (p.243): symbolic action has the same ambiguous potentialities; actual conflicts can be transcended (results sometimes fatal, sometimes felicitous); but Burke prefers DRAMATISTIC to DIALECTICAL because dialectic has lost track of its dramatistic origins. Image-as-attitude paragraph: images can have force of attitudes; lyric analogue of plot can be tracked in the progression of imagery (Shelley's Ode to the West Wind worked example, pp.243-245 — five-stanza arc with abyssal stanza-three imagery of submerged vegetation; the Wordsworth Westminster Bridge sonnet contrasts as PURE LYRIC of arrested-summarization). Drama vs lyric distinction (p.245): from the dramatic point of view, the attitude is a PRE-ACT; from the lyric point of view, the attitude is a SUMMATION (transcending overt action by symbolically encompassing its end). Hamlet (pp.247): Hamlet's poignancy comes from transforming preparations-for-action into devices-for-postponing-action — Shakespeare nearly dissolves drama into pre-action-that-amounts-to-no-action, opposite to O'Neill's Mourning Becomes Electra dissolution of agent into stimulus-response. Rhetorical-level closing: legislatures adopt the 'Hamletic strategy' of appointing fact-finding committees to forestall vote ('Hamlet being the first great liberal').

outline.title: Realist Family and Nominalist Aggregate (Korzybski's nominalist abstraction-ladder vs realist tribal-substance; Plato; Aristotelian entelechy; Duns Scotus haecceitas)
outline.summary: Burke returns to Korzybski's 'consciousness of abstracting' but now from a GRAMMATICAL angle. Korzybski's method ('table' abstracts because it applies to a vast aggregate of objects each different in particulars; 'furniture' abstracts further; up through 'conveniences,' 'commodities,' 'things,' 'objects,' 'being') is characteristically scientist and NOMINALIST (Baldwin: nominalism = 'doctrine that universals have no objective existence or validity' — universals are 'creations of language for purposes of convenient communication'). REALIST Grammar works the other way: it begins with a tribal concept and treats individuals as participants in this common substance/element. Burke's signature formula (p.248): REALISM TREATS INDIVIDUALS AS MEMBERS OF A GROUP; NOMINALISM TREATS GROUPS AS AGGREGATES OF INDIVIDUALS. The realistic pattern fits clan-origin Greek democracy and Western feudal familial patterns. Plato treats the perfect idea of a chair as the reality with individuals imperfectly participating; Aristotle by his theory of the ENTELECHY achieves the same act-genus-generation tie-up in his uncreated world ('the striving of each thing to be perfectly the kind of thing it was'). Scientist-explains-abstraction-via-nouns; dramatist-stress-on-act suggests origin in VERBS (run, go, do are abstract and general; nouns/proper-names individuate). Realism's key word was BEING or ESSENCE — a VERBAL noun, the most abstract and general form of the most abstract and general act. Essence/quiddity as 'a way' (Shakespeare 'has a way with him' = his literary style = his essence as poet); animalitas, rationalitas (Santayana's 'life of reason'); rationality is tribal + formal + an act. Duns Scotus on HAECCEITAS (thisness) — surface-nominalistic but retains tribal familial pattern: si loquamur realiter, humanitas quae est in Socrate non est humanitas quae est in Platone (Socrates has a different humanity than Plato; locate his essence in special socratitas). Closing paragraph: contemporary 'scientific realism' is sometimes euphemistic for materialism, sometimes pragmatism-like, sometimes rhetoric-of-unmasking, sometimes jurisprudential. Nominalism is 'anti-social' grammatically: if carried out consistently it obliterates all consubstantiality and leaves us 'with a world of individuals, united only by monetary symbols and the deceptions of an idealistic rhetoric.'

outline.title: Further Remarks on Act and Potency (un-Aristotelian appreciation of Aristotle; Platonism as transcendent ante rem realism; Aristotle's entelechy as in rebus; pure act / motionless mover / form-matter hierarchy; ratio as potential-to-actual formula; Heisenberg digression)
outline.summary: Methodological caveat opens: 'Our appreciation of Aristotle is itself un-Aristotelian; our remarks about Aquinas would not satisfy a Thomist' — Burke is reviewing dialectical resources from the dramatist standpoint, not arguing for one traditional application. Modern science asks how acts are motivated; Aristotelian science tells how motions are activated. Platonism left motivation in 'tribal' stage with universal ante rem (transcendent; pure-form idea of family in heaven, individuals imperfectly partaking on earth). Aristotelian entelechy resides in sensory things (in rebus): 'Actuality is prior both to potency and to every principle of change.' Plato-as-statement-about-language paragraph: Plato's heavenly archetypes are 'sound enough, if read as a statement about the relationship between class names and names for the individuals thus classified by a common essence' — Korzybski's contribution is 'having said alas!' to an aspect of linguistic transcendence Plato considered edifying. Aristotle's metaphysics 'more dialectical than Plato's' in the sense that Plato used dialectic as a means to the end of truth, while Aristotle isolated method (formal logic) AND attributed dialectical structure to the very nature of the universe. Form-matter HIERARCHY paragraph (pp.253-254): forms arranged as a hierarchy with the form of beings at each level constituting the matter of beings at the next higher level, ascending until you arrive at 'pure form,' the motionless prime mover that moves all else by being loved, the object of desire. Burke's action-motion translation: each order of being constitutes the conditions-of-motion involved in the action of the next higher order (human action depends on animal motion; animal action depends on vegetative motion; vegetative action depends on physical motion). REVERSIBILITY of pure act as final cause: motions toward it might be interpreted as motions derived from it (final cause = efficient cause), particularly when theologians took over Aristotle's God and restored the generative principle. Mystics distinguish egressus from God and regressus to God (the OXYMORON of joined moments). Aquinas's two-directions formula: God is present in things (1) after the manner of efficient cause ('equivocally,' as 'in the sun is the likeness of whatever is generated by the sun's power') and (2) as object of operation is in operator. Macrocosm-microcosm + omnia ubique synecdochic ground. The matter-as-substrate (hypokeimenon = placed-beneath, subject) discussion: BOTH members of the potentiality-actuality pair are tinged by the paradox of substance. God-as-pure-act takes grammatical form of PASSIVE (object of desire); matter as Windelband's 'impulse to be formed' is characterized as POTENCY — 'what passivity ever possessed more active a name?' Seed-rot vs radish-seed examples; rationes seminales; Deus implicitus / Deus explicitus mystical world-pantheism; Leibniz monads as pre-formed possibilities; 'the unconscious is virtually (potentially) the conscious.' Lombroso 'criminaloid' and legal-theory 'potentialities for committing crime' as bad-faith potentiality-actuality machinery. The TENDENCY paragraph: social sciences cannot do without 'tendency' (and its caeteris-paribus + mutatis-mutandis Janus-terms); a tendency is ambiguous because mere tendency-to-do is also tendency-not-to-do; Frank Knight Ethics of Competition perfect-market 'tendency' example. INEVITABILITY-vs-TENDENCY distinction: deterministic 'inevitable' substantially merges permanent and changing (Marxist proletariat's 'inevitable' development claim). Dramatic suspense / historical inevitability formal-substantiality parallel ('the ending is implicit in the beginning'). Heisenberg digression (pp.259-260): instruments are profoundly Grammatical, cannot get past paradox of substance; 'A margin of indeterminacy is inevitable in measurement' refines Zeno; no logical necessity to conclude that indeterminacy is intrinsic to nature itself. Brehier's scholastic proportion: existence is to essence as act is to potency. Aristotle's actuality-prior-to-potency: temporal sense (one actuality always precedes another in time right back to the eternal prime mover); FORM-and-substantiality sense (man is prior to boy because man has attained complete form). Entelechy = 'having its end within itself' as synonym for actuality; teleios (perfect / complete / having attributes of an end) = both 'completed man' and infinite God; poiema's deed-doing-action / made-work ambiguity. Closing return-to-ratio paragraph (p.262): the 10 ratios become 20 because reversible; A RATIO IS A FORMULA INDICATING A TRANSITION FROM ONE TERM TO ANOTHER, and the mediated necessarily differs from the immediate as translation differs from original — every ratio has POTENTIAL-TO-ACTUAL form.

outline.title: Psychology of Action (action-passion + actus-status + action-motion + potential as the four motivational pairs; Spinoza; Eliot's Murder in the Cathedral; Hegelian Spirit; Stoic hegemonikon; Rousseau; psychoanalysis exegesis; Indo-European middle voice; pivot to Agency)
outline.summary: Final subsection re-maps the entire chapter as a typology of motivational pairs (action-passion; actus-status; action-motion ambiguity; the potential). Active/passive 'are but names for bins into which one sorts various kinds of particulars' (Spinoza's affections differ from any other philosopher's alignment). A dramatist might select any two ethical motives (fear and honor) and enact them as the interrelation-and-transformation of active and passive principles. Characters rarely speak the dramatist Grammar specifically — Eliot's Murder in the Cathedral St Thomas is exception (Eliot's Dante/theology interest); the turning-wheel image equates action and passion; The Dry Salvages: 'Where action were otherwise movement / Of that which is only moved / And has in it no source of movement — Driven by daemonic, chthonic / Powers.' Lear's 'more sinned against than sinning' = ingredients of passion in a sin-grammar with active form. Japanese WWII propaganda exhibit: active-drawing-the-enemy-closer vs passive-suffering-attack; German 'advancing Westward' retreat-language. Poiema-pathema-mathema temporal series: action organizes resistant factors which call forth passion; moment of transcendence arises when sufferer (originally seeing unenlightened) is enabled to see in more comprehensive terms modified by suffering. Christian martyrdom: act of self-sacrifice IS the sufferance (act-passion as simultaneous-equivalents); Eliot's Saint suffers temptation (pathema), resists (poiema), the trial's understanding (mathema) equips him for martyrdom (new action-passion level). GODS-AS-TRIBAL-MOTIVES: par excellence dramatist grammar; tribal-identity-uppermost makes supernatural vocabulary feel adequate (guilt = tribal judgment = pursuit by Furies has external existence); individualism reverses the development (psychologists begin with ego, treat tribal motives as super-ego; Jung's collective unconscious reaffirms tribal). Ruling-passion theory (Tacitus, Theophrastus, biography of biography): an oxymoron — 'dominant subjection / sovereign bondage.' Ben Jonson Every Man out of his Humour: humour as liquid → bodily liquid → state of mind → kind of dramatic form (Volpone: 'What a rare punishment / Is avarice to itself!'). Hegel's Absolute Spirit using blind passions of men as its medium (world-historical individual). FREEDOM as dialectical term (pp.267-268): Aristotle's freedom as 'liberal art' (free man = exists for own sake) NOT in opposition to authority — participant in authoritative structure (intellect controlling enslaving passions). Modern freedom as polemic/propagandistic doctrine of partial slaves in partial revolt — middle-class slogan, stress on service and utility. Stoic hegemonikon (rule of reason = rule of self = rule of state) — partial shattering by Rousseau's 'necessity in things' over 'caprices of other men.' Spinoza's anti-Hobbesian naturalism implications. ACTUS-STATUS transformation: a 'ruling class' can become transformed from class-that-does to class-that-does-not — substantiality of properties inheriting independently of generating act. Christian paradox (pp.271-272): 'passionals' or 'acts' for martyrdom-accounts; suffering as act; willing-one's-subjection making submission an act because sufferance is an act; universalizing servitude (all men slaves of God, hence none substantially slaves, hence respect-as-persons). Psychology exegesis (p.269): frustration / fixation / complex = passion; adjustment / normality = action; sublimation = transcendence; repression / inhibition = new dialectic of reason-as-hegemonikon. McDougall's sentiments require placement as 'incipient action.' Closing (pp.273-274) — INDO-EUROPEAN MIDDLE-VOICE GRAMMAR: Aristotle (Physics I.6-7) asks 'whether the basic principles of nature are two or three or some greater number' — active/passive opposition + underlying-substratum mediating third (the bronze-to-statue / wood-to-bed analogy = potentiality). Grammatically: the passive voice is a LATE Indo-European development; originally active and middle (reflexive); passive evolved from middle (Greek middle and passive conjugations are alike in many tenses). Passive forms 'probably indicate a high degree of development from actus to status, with a corresponding increase in the sense of mental states.' Caldwell/Hemingway sparse-behavioristic narrative as post-passive sophisticated sensitivity. Final pivot sentence: the reflexive moves in the direction of means and will be considered under Agency. 'We have now considered the big three, scene, agent, and act. We shall now consider the remaining two, Agency and Purpose, that draw together in the means-ends relationship.'

act_term_operationalization.operational_definition_burke_faithful: ACT is the pentad term answering the grammatical question 'what was done?' On the realist construal Burke develops in this chapter, an act is an actualization — the bringing of a potentiality (dynamis) into full realization (energeia) in accordance with a form proper to its kind. An act has internal directionality (entelechy = having its end within itself), is reciprocally related to potency, is distinguishable from mere motion (which lies in the realm of instruments), and admits a spectrum of intermediate states (attitude, incipient act, delayed act).

decision_rules: If a vocabulary derives motive from actualization in accordance with form-of-kind, classify as featuring Act.
If a vocabulary places motive-locus in heavenly Idea (transcendent universal), classify as Platonist realism (still Act-featuring but via ante rem mechanism).
If a vocabulary places motive-locus in in-things entelechy, classify as Aristotelian realism (in rebus).
If a vocabulary reduces act to motion (no internal source of movement), it has crossed the action-motion watershed and is no longer dramatist — flag as operationalist / scenic-reduction.
If a vocabulary treats action as substitute for or beginning of overt action, it is in incipient-act territory — symbolic action and rhetoric live here.
If a vocabulary names a verbal noun (being, essence, quiddity) as fundamental, that vocabulary is realist by Burke's verbal-noun-as-most-abstract-act test.

If a vocabulary classifies first by individual-things-then-aggregates, classify as nominalist (not realist-Act-featuring); if it classifies first by tribal/familial substance then derives individuals, classify as realist.

aristotle_exegesis_table.burke_exegetical_move: Establishes energeia/actu/actuality as the defining-mark of the real and the chapter's central anchor; uses Metaphysics IX as the locus for the potentiality-actuality reciprocity Burke needs for his incipient-act apparatus; deploys actuality-prior-to-potency as the Aristotelian inversion of the seed-precedes-plant intuition; flags the action-motion ambiguity (energeia 'extended from movements to other things') as the watershed-moment dividing dramatism from operationalism
aristotle_exegesis_table.centrality: PRIMARY — most-cited Aristotelian work in the chapter

aristotle_exegesis_table.burke_passage: pp.273-274 (the Physics I.6-7 active/passive/underlying-substratum block — 'whether the basic principles of nature are two or three or some greater number')
aristotle_exegesis_table.burke_exegetical_move: Closes the chapter by using Aristotle's question about the number of basic principles of nature as a GRAMMATICAL-VOICE question — whether active/passive opposition needs a mediating middle-voice ground; Burke then jumps to Indo-European philology to argue that passive voice is a late development from middle voice (closing pivot to Agency)
aristotle_exegesis_table.centrality: PRIMARY at chapter close (the literal pivot to Agency)

aristotle_exegesis_table.burke_passage: pp.230-231 (long block-quotation from Poetics 6 'Tragedy is essentially an imitation not of persons but of action and life...' + immediate alignment of the six tragic elements with Burke's five pentad terms)
aristotle_exegesis_table.burke_exegetical_move: PENTAD-AS-SIX-ELEMENTS MAPPING — plot=Act, character=Agent, thought=Purpose, melody+diction=Agency, spectacle=Scene (as scenic agency); reads the Poetics' designation of plot as the foremost element of tragedy as evidence of Aristotle's act-featuring grammar; uses the Poetics' end-of-action-is-activity-not-quality as warrant for treating Aristotle's God (pure act / unmoved mover) as conceived dramatically (as end-of-action) even though paradoxically lyrical (perfect rest)
aristotle_exegesis_table.centrality: PRIMARY — the Poetics block is one of the chapter's two longest verbatim quotations

aristotle_exegesis_table.burke_passage: p.227 (Aquinas's comment on Aristotle's Metaphysics referring to the soul as 'the act of an organic physical body capable of life')
aristotle_exegesis_table.burke_exegetical_move: Uses Aristotle's hylomorphic definition of soul (filtered through Aquinas's commentary) as the chapter's strongest example of the actus-essence identity — soul is literally the act of a body, not a substance separate from a body; this is the chapter's deepest anchor for the dissertation's affective-layer crosswalk (soul-as-act ↔ embodied affordance / Wirkmal-Merkmal closing of functional circle)
aristotle_exegesis_table.centrality: SECONDARY but theoretically load-bearing for the dissertation bridge

aristotle_exegesis_table.burke_passage: p.230 (Aristotle on action as the end of human life — 'the end for which we live is a certain kind of activity, not a quality' — drawn from the Poetics-Ethics adjacency) + p.267 (Aristotle's metaphysics as a 'liberal art' where the free man 'exists for his own sake and not for another's')
aristotle_exegesis_table.burke_exegetical_move: Uses Aristotelian eudaimonia-as-activity (without naming eudaimonia) to anchor the act-as-end-not-quality formula; uses the liberal-arts-free-man passage to distinguish Aristotelian freedom (participant in authoritative structure, intellect over enslaving passions) from modern protest-freedom
aristotle_exegesis_table.centrality: SECONDARY (less direct than Metaphysics/Poetics) but supplies the chapter's Politics-flavored material on freedom

aristotle_exegesis_table.burke_passage: p.267 ('the most architectonic and authoritative science...like slave-women may not even contradict it'; Aristotelian freedom in the class of free men vs slaves)
aristotle_exegesis_table.burke_exegetical_move: Reads the Politics-flavored architectonic-science passage as confirmation of Aristotle's non-revolutionary freedom; uses Aristotelian slavery as a foil for Stoic universalization of servitude and Christian transvaluation of slavery into voluntary submission
aristotle_exegesis_table.centrality: TERTIARY but functional in the Psychology-of-Action exegesis of action-passion / freedom-servitude pairs

aristotle_exegesis_table.burke_passage: p.228 (Aristotle's studies of logic 'traditionally go under the name of the Organon (that is, tool or instrument)')
aristotle_exegesis_table.burke_exegetical_move: Uses the Organon-as-instrument etymology to argue that even though Aristotle omits agency as a fifth cause, his treatment of logic-as-tool 'clearly enough takes it into account' — i.e. Aristotle's terminology is implicitly five-term even where explicitly four-term
aristotle_exegesis_table.centrality: TERTIARY but elegant — supplies the chapter's argument that the pentad is grammatically pre-fitted to Aristotelian science

aquinas_exegesis.burke_passage: p.227 ('Likeness of Creatures' discussion: 'It is of the nature of action that a like agent should produce a like action, since every thing acts according as it is in act')
aquinas_exegesis.burke_exegetical_move: Establishes the AGENT-ACT RATIO as scholastic realism's primary ratio — agent and act are mutually constituting; Aquinas's distinction between God-as-cause and human-agents-as-effect (transcendent disproportion) is read as preserving the ratio while differentiating substantial-similarity (univocal) from analogical-similarity (equivocal)

aquinas_exegesis.thomist_work: Aquinas on Aristotle's four causes (Everyman's Library edition, pp.154-163)
aquinas_exegesis.burke_passage: pp.228-229 (the chapter's pentad-as-four-causes mapping is constructed by READING Aquinas READING Aristotle)
aquinas_exegesis.burke_exegetical_move: Burke calls this commentary 'the most convenient place I know for directly observing the essentially dramatist nature of both Aristotle and Aquinas' — the source-text for the chapter's PENTAD-AS-FOUR-CAUSES MAPPING (material=Scene, efficient=Agent, final=Purpose, formal=Act, with agency incidental); also the source for the Ibn-Sina auxiliary-efficient-cause four-fold expansion read as agent/agency overlap

Reads Aquinas's two-directions formula as RESOLVING the Aristotelian-mystical tension between God-as-source (efficient cause) and God-as-end (final cause): God-in-things either as equivocal-cause (sun-likeness analogy) or as object-of-operation

aquinas_exegesis.thomist_work: Summa Theologica (implicit — via Gilson's God and Philosophy)
aquinas_exegesis.burke_passage: p.227 (Etienne Gilson on existence as 'an act, not a thing'; footnote on the copulative verb being grammatically active)
aquinas_exegesis.burke_exegetical_move: Uses Gilson's reading of the Thomist existential act-of-being as warrant for the realist Grammar's act-featuring; the sociological footnote ('this identification between act and being served a feudal society built upon the maintenance of fixed social status') is Burke's signature move of locating a metaphysics within its material conditions

aquinas_exegesis.thomist_work: Aquinas's treatment of essence/existence distinction (Baldwin dictionary report)
aquinas_exegesis.burke_passage: p.227 (Baldwin: existence as 'the act of essence')
aquinas_exegesis.burke_exegetical_move: Uses the dictionary's compressed report of the essence-existence distinction to set up the chapter's Brehier-cited scholastic proportion (p.261: 'existence is to essence as act is to potency') — a formula Burke then uses to interrogate the matter-potentiality equation

incipient_act_apparatus.label: incipient/delayed act
incipient_act_apparatus.burke_definition: An incipient act is a perception/attitude that contains the form of a not-yet-actualized act — Richards' 'preliminary adjustments, getting ready to act' or Mead's 'beginnings of acts.' The incipient act is fundamentally AMBIGUOUS: an attitude can be substitute for an act OR first step toward an act. The realm of the incipient is the realm of SYMBOLIC ACTION par excellence — actual conflicts can be transcended there, with results sometimes fatal, sometimes felicitous.
philosophical_genealogy: Aristotle Metaphysics IX (potentiality-actuality reciprocity; 'every potency is at one and the same time a potency of the opposite')

Korzybski Science and Sanity (delayed response; consciousness of abstracting)
Coleridge on empathy (Venus and Adonis shooting-star)

dissertation_crosslinks.anchor: Calleja's three-moment micro-phase (Ch.3 ergodicity definition) is structurally homologous to Burke's incipient/actualized/transcended act; Calleja's microtactic = Burke's incipient act in the moment-of-action limit

concepts.label: act (canonical pentad-featured term)
concepts.gloss: Burke's pentad term answering 'what was done?'; on realist construal = actualization of potency in accordance with form-of-kind; reciprocally related to potency; distinguishable from motion.

concepts.label: energeia / actu / actuality
concepts.anchor: p.227 (Baldwin citing Aristotle: 'things are more or less real according as they are more or less energeia (actu)')
concepts.gloss: Aristotelian term for actualization-as-mark-of-reality; the Greek root ergon = work/deed; Burke's primary etymological anchor for Act.

concepts.label: dynamis / potency / potentiality
concepts.gloss: Reciprocal of actuality; every potency is potency of the opposite (Metaphysics IX.8); matter is the realm of potentiality; in being potentially good, matter is potentially bad; potentiality has two species — tendency (ambiguous, can-go-either-way) and inevitability (substantial-merging-of-permanent-and-changing).

concepts.label: entelechy ('having its end within itself')
concepts.gloss: Aristotle's synonym for actuality; the principle that each kind of thing strives to be perfectly the kind of thing it is; resides in things (in rebus) rather than transcendently (ante rem); Aristotle's modification of Platonist realism that allowed inductive study of genera/species.

concepts.label: form / formal cause = Act
concepts.gloss: Aristotle's formal cause ('the form or pattern, the formula of the essence') = Burke's term Act; 'a form is an act'; quidditas / whatness; record-of-an-act-which-gave-it-form.

concepts.label: four causes pentad-mapping (material-Scene / efficient-Agent / final-Purpose / formal-Act / agency-incidental)
concepts.gloss: Chapter's most explicit cross-walk: Aristotle's four causes ALIGNED with Burke's pentad. Material=Scene (bronze of statue), Efficient=Agent (initial origin of change), Final=Purpose (end for which a thing is), Formal=Act (form / pattern / formula of essence). Agency is incidental in Aristotle (Organon = tool/instrument).

concepts.label: Aquinas Ibn-Sina auxiliary-efficient-cause = agent/agency overlap
concepts.gloss: Aquinas's four varieties of efficient cause include an 'auxiliary' or 'secondary' agent that acts for another's ends (soldier directed by statesman; universe-of-nature as secondary-agent of supreme-mind primary-agent); marks the overlap of agent and agency for Burke.

concepts.label: scholastic hexameter (quis, quid, ubi, quibus auxiliis, cur, quo modo, quando)
concepts.gloss: Burke's NEGATIVE-WAY confirmation of pentad-as-four-causes. Quis=Agent, ubi+quando=Scene, cur=Purpose, quibus auxiliis+quo modo=Agency, quid=Act (and form-of-thing was called quidditas).

concepts.label: Aristotle's God / pure act / unmoved mover
concepts.gloss: Conceived dramatistically as end-of-action; paradox-of-absolute: pure act is like no act at all (perfect repose); motivates as a passive (loved or desired, eromenon); takes grammatical form of passive voice; lyrical (perfect rest) not dramatic; God-source / God-end distinction enabled mystical egressus/regressus oxymoron.

concepts.label: soul as 'act of an organic physical body capable of life' (Aquinas on De Anima)
concepts.gloss: Burke's strongest single example of actus-essence identity — soul is literally the act of a body, not a substance separable from a body; hylomorphic anchor for embodied-affordance / Wirkmal-Merkmal dissertation bridge.

concepts.label: Aristotle's six tragic elements aligned with pentad (Poetics)
concepts.gloss: Plot=Act, Character=Agent, Thought=Purpose, Melody+Diction=Agency, Spectacle=Scene-as-scenic-agency. Tragedy is 'imitation not of persons but of action and life'; plot is the foremost element.

concepts.label: the pathetic fallacy (Ruskin / Miss Miles)
concepts.gloss: Attribution of human emotions to non-human objects ('the trees were gay, the mountains mourned'). Miss Miles's restricted definition tracks scene-agent (lyric) ratio; Burke EXTENDS to cover the broader action-motion ambiguity (motion-personalization-as-act).

concepts.label: motion-action ambiguity / action-motion watershed (extended pathetic fallacy)
concepts.gloss: Burke's signature methodological apparatus from this chapter: motion (instrumental, scientific, scene-reducible) vs action (dramatistic, with internal source). 'The wheat tossed in the wind' (motion) vs 'the wheat tossed its head in the wind' (action). The watershed moment dividing dramatism from operationalism.

concepts.label: policy-making function (proverbial realism vs managerial idealism)
concepts.gloss: Active or policy-making function integral to vocabularies of motivation; realistic when arising from tribal experience (proverbs); tending toward idealism when derived from managerial agents (government functionaries); requires correctives of materialist criticism.

concepts.label: incipient act (Richards' Principles of Literary Criticism)
concepts.gloss: Perception as 'response in the form of incipient action'; preliminary adjustments, getting ready to act; symbolic representation arouses imaginal activities and tendencies-to-action without overt action being called for; Richards values incipient-act-staying-incipient as sign of intelligence/refinement.

concepts.label: incipient-act ambiguity (substitute-for-act vs first-step-toward-act)
concepts.gloss: Burke's CENTRAL EXTENSION of Richards: the incipient act is fundamentally ambiguous — an attitude can be substitute for an act OR first step toward an act. Rhetoric of advertisers and propagandists exploits this ambiguity.

concepts.label: attitude as 'beginning of acts' (Mead Mind Self and Society)
concepts.gloss: Mead's formulation of incipient action; The Philosophy of the Act re-readable as The Philosophy of the Attitude (if we remember Mead's concern is with incipient-as-introductory rather than incipient-as-substitutive).

concepts.label: vocal gesture (Mead)
concepts.gloss: Mead's language-as-vocal-gestures: we arouse in ourselves the attitudes language serves to arouse in others; adopting 'attitude of the other' in formation of moral consciousness.

concepts.label: Meadian action-minus / attitude-minus (organism-confronting-resistance)
concepts.gloss: Mead's action does not involve rationality or consciousness; equated with internal motivations of organism encountering external resistance; analogous to Santayana's 'field of action'; halfway between motion and action.

concepts.label: Mead's self as social-attitude complex / Hegelian dialectic of Spirit-alienated-as-Nature
concepts.gloss: Mead's self emerges as the individual learns the 'attitude of the other'; the individual takes the attitude of resisting his own attitude in grasping (anticipating object-resistance); complexity of social attitudes built atop biological motives; Hegelian-dialectic pattern.

concepts.label: delayed response (Korzybski Science and Sanity)
concepts.gloss: Korzybski's technique for delaying every response because explanations are askew; primary concern with criticism of language as social instrument; would have us delay every response. Burke: Korzybski works better as Rhetoric than Grammar.

concepts.label: consciousness of abstracting (Korzybski)
concepts.gloss: Korzybski's signature concept: programmatic awareness that every term abstracts and classifies (chair1, chair2, chair3 vs generic 'chair'). Burke: a haphazardly rediscovered aspect of Neo-Platonism; calls for expansion into a consciousness of dialectic in general; characteristically scientist and nominalist method.

concepts.label: poiema / pathema / mathema (Greek dramatist-action triplet)
concepts.gloss: Burke's Greek-grammar triplet of action / suffering / learning. Chair example: 'by participation in the Korzybski mathema, through the medium of a delayed poiema we may avoid a disconcerting pathema.' Christian martyrdom: pathema (temptation) + poiema (resistance) + mathema (understanding) = martyrdom as new action-passion level.

concepts.label: symbolic action (realm of the incipient/attitudinal par excellence)
concepts.gloss: Symbolic action has the same ambiguous potentialities of action when tested by norms of overt practical action; the area of thought wherein actual conflicts can be transcended (sometimes fatal, sometimes felicitous). Burke prefers 'dramatistic' to 'dialectical' because dialectic has lost track of its dramatistic origins.

concepts.label: image-as-attitude / lyric-analogue-of-plot (image-progression)
concepts.gloss: Images can have force of attitudes; lyric structure (which has no act in the full dramatic sense) can be analyzed by tracking the progression/development of imagery (abyssal middle stanza in Shelley's West Wind; pure-arrest Wordsworth Westminster Bridge sonnet).

concepts.label: drama vs lyric (pre-act vs summation-of-action)
concepts.gloss: From dramatic POV the moment of arrest is a PRE-ACT (preparation for action); from lyric POV it is a SUMMATION (transcending overt action by symbolically encompassing its end). Aristotle's world is dramatic; his God (pure act = perfect rest) is lyrical.

concepts.label: Hamletic strategy (preparations-as-postponements)
concepts.gloss: Hamlet transforms preparations-for-action into devices-for-postponing-action; Shakespeare nearly dissolves drama into pre-action-amounting-to-no-action (opposite extreme to O'Neill's dissolution of agent into stimulus-response). Legislatures adopt the Hamletic strategy by appointing fact-finding committees ('Hamlet being the first great liberal').

concepts.label: realism (Burke's signature formula: treats individuals as members of a group)
concepts.gloss: Realism begins with tribal/familial concept and treats individuals as participants in common substance/element; fits clan-origin Greek democracy and Western feudal familial patterns. KEY FORMULA: 'realism treats individuals as members of a group, whereas nominalism treats groups as aggregates of individuals.'

concepts.label: nominalism (treats groups as aggregates of individuals)
concepts.gloss: Baldwin: 'doctrine that universals have no objective existence or validity'; universals are 'creations of language for purposes of convenient communication.' Occam: 'positive assertion that specific individualities, differentiated in themselves, are the real.' Korzybski's method is characteristically nominalist.

concepts.label: act-genus-generation tie-up (realist's grammatical reason for Act-featuring)
concepts.gloss: If world is either result-of-enactment (Plato) or process-of-enactment (Aristotle), act-form-generation mutually involve one another; each genus carries out one line of generation/actualization. Aristotle achieves this in uncreated world via entelechy. Verbal-noun-as-most-abstract-act test: realism's key word 'being/essence' is verbal noun.

concepts.label: essence as 'a way' (essence/quiddity-as-kind-of-action)
concepts.gloss: 'He has a way with him' = quality/aptitude peculiarly his own = principle of his character = essence. Shakespeare 'has a way with him' = his literary style = essence of Shakespeare as poet. Generic words like animalitas, rationalitas name a 'way' (kind of action) — Santayana's 'life of reason.'

concepts.label: haecceitas (Duns Scotus' thisness)
concepts.gloss: Surface-nominalistic but retains tribal-familial pattern of scholasticism. 'Si loquamur realiter, humanitas quae est in Socrate non est humanitas quae est in Platone.' Socrates has different humanity than Plato; his essence resides in special socratitas — individual treated AS A GENUS.

concepts.label: scientific realism (jurisprudential vs materialist vs pragmatist senses)
concepts.gloss: Sometimes euphemism for materialism (scenic factors narrowed circumference); sometimes aspect of pragmatism; sometimes rhetoric-of-unmasking false idealizations; in jurisprudence combines features with act-featuring stress.

concepts.label: Aristotelian actuality-prior-to-potentiality
concepts.gloss: Aristotle's principle: 'Actuality is prior both to potency and to every principle of change.' Temporal sense (one actuality always precedes another in time back to eternal prime mover); form-and-substantiality sense (man is prior to boy because man has attained complete form). Geometer-discovers-potencies-by-actualizing example.

concepts.label: form-matter hierarchy / orders-of-being / motionless prime mover
concepts.gloss: Forms arranged as hierarchy with form of beings at each level constituting matter of beings at next higher level, ascending to pure form (motionless prime mover that moves all else by being loved). Burke's action-motion translation: each order's motion constitutes conditions for next-higher-order's action (human action depends on animal motion, animal action on vegetative motion, etc.).

concepts.label: reversibility of pure act (final cause = efficient cause)
concepts.gloss: Motions toward pure act might be interpreted as motions derived from it (final cause = efficient cause), particularly when theologians restored generative principle. Mystical egressus from God / regressus to God as oxymoron of joined moments. Aquinas's two-directions formula: God-in-things as equivocal-efficient-cause (sun-likeness analogy) and as object-of-operation-in-operator.

concepts.label: matter as substrate (hypokeimenon, placed-beneath, subject)
concepts.gloss: Burke's etymology: hypokeimenon = the placed-beneath, or 'subject'; possesses potentialities that may be variously actualized; Windelband's phrase: 'impulse to be formed'; characterized as potency. Paradox: God-as-pure-act takes grammatical form of passive (object of desire); matter takes 'active' name (potency).

concepts.label: implicit-to-explicit / Deus implicitus / Deus explicitus / Leibnizian monad as pre-formed seed
concepts.gloss: Implicit:explicit::potential:actual proportion. Mystical world-pantheism: development from Deus implicitus to Deus explicitus (nature is God-made-manifest). Leibniz monads as pre-formed possibilities. Modern psychology rephrase: 'the unconscious is virtually (potentially) the conscious.'

concepts.label: tendency (ambiguous potentiality)
concepts.gloss: A 'tendency' is fundamentally ambiguous because tendency-to-do is also tendency-not-to-do. Frank Knight Ethics of Competition perfect-market example: the ideal market is a direction toward which Knight would have the actual market 'tend'; caeteris-paribus and mutatis-mutandis Janus-terms. Cannot be embarrassed if the tendency remains unactualized.

concepts.label: inevitability (substantial-merging-of-permanent-and-changing)
concepts.gloss: Strict-determinism / predestination / historically-inevitable potentiality. Substantially merges permanent and changing; accounts for flux by an underlying principle that prevails always; says in effect not simply that future will be but that it IS, since implicit in present. Marxist proletariat's 'inevitable' development claim shares this substantiality. Dramatic suspense / historical inevitability formal-substantiality parallel.

concepts.label: ratio as potential-to-actual formula (10 ratios → 20 reversible ratios)
concepts.gloss: All 10 pentadic dyads are reversible: a mode of thought in keeping with the scene-agent ratio situates in scene certain potentialities actualized in agent; the agent-scene ratio reverses. List expands to 20. 'A ratio is a formula indicating a transition from one term to another'; the mediated necessarily differs from the immediate as translation differs from original.

concepts.label: action-passion pair
concepts.gloss: First and most basic of the chapter's four motivational pairs. Active and passive are 'but names for bins into which one sorts various kinds of particulars' (Spinoza's affections). Dramatist enacts ethical motives as interrelations and transformations of active and passive principles. Christian martyrdom: act-of-self-sacrifice identical with sufferance.

concepts.label: actus-status pair
concepts.gloss: Second motivational pair. 'A ruling class can become transformed from a class that does to a class that does not' — substantiality of properties inheriting independently of generating act. Passive forms in Indo-European indicate high degree of development from actus to status. Echoes substance-vocabulary work in GM-02.

concepts.label: Indo-European middle voice / passive-from-middle origin
concepts.gloss: Closing-chapter philological argument: in Indo-European family the passive voice is a late development; originally only active and middle (reflexive) forms existed; passive evolved from middle (Greek middle and passive conjugations are alike in many tenses); prior to development passive ideas were expressed actively-but-reflexively (action directed by self upon self).

concepts.label: Stoic hegemonikon (reason as authority-equation)
concepts.gloss: Stoic reason-authority equation links idea of private rule with idea of public rule. Aristotle's freedom is participant in authoritative structure (intellect controlling enslaving passions), NOT in opposition to authority. Modern freedom partial-shattering by Rousseau's necessity-in-things over caprices-of-other-men.

concepts.label: Christian transvaluation of suffering as act (passional / acts)
concepts.gloss: Christianity offered doctrine whereby subjects were persons capable of action in their passion; willing-one's-subjection made submission an act because sufferance was an act. Universalizing servitude: all men slaves of God, hence none substantially slaves, hence respect-as-persons. Combines with Aristotelian free-person concept.

concepts.label: psychoanalysis-as-dramatist-Grammar exegesis
concepts.gloss: Burke's exegetical formula: frustration / fixation / complex = passion; adjustment / normality = action; sublimation = transcendence; repression / inhibition = new dialectic of reason as hegemonikon (stated in quizzical terms whereas formerly stated unambiguously favorable). Not asking modern psychology to abandon its terms — asking ourselves to apply such exegesis.

concepts.label: gods as tribal motives (par excellence dramatist grammar)
concepts.gloss: Gods considered as motives are an active vocabulary for naming mental processes and 'mechanisms.' Tribal-identity-uppermost makes supernatural vocabulary feel adequate (guilt = tribal judgment = pursuit by Furies). Individualism reverses development (ego / super-ego; Jung's collective unconscious reaffirms tribal).

concepts.label: Aristotle's 'freedom as liberal art' (NOT in opposition to authority)
concepts.gloss: Aristotle in Metaphysics: 'as the man is free, who exists for his own sake and not for another's, so we pursue this as the only free science.' Architectonic and authoritative science. Aristotelian freedom is non-revolutionary; participant in authoritative structure. Modern freedom as polemic doctrine of partial slaves in partial revolt.

concepts.label: an act would be possible only to a ruler or ruling class (Burke's political-grammatical claim)
concepts.gloss: Considered solely in terms of political power, an 'act' would be possible only to ruler/ruling-class. Applied by analogy to psychology of individual: act would be possible only to part of soul enjoying corresponding status of authority — the Stoic hegemonikon located in reason.

positions.label: Realism features Act because act-genus-generation form a mutually-involving tie-up
positions.anchor: pp.247-249 (Realist Family and Nominalist Aggregate subsection)
positions.claim: If one thinks of the world either as the result of enactment (Plato) or itself a process of enactment (Aristotle), one begins with an act-genus-generation tie-up which can indicate why on the Grammatical level traditional realism favors the term Act. Aristotle's entelechy achieves this tie-up in his uncreated world (each thing striving to be perfectly the kind of thing it is).

positions.label: The motion-action ambiguity is the watershed-moment dividing dramatism from operationalism
positions.claim: Burke extends the pathetic fallacy from Miss Miles's restricted attribute-of-emotion definition to the wider action-motion ambiguity. This watershed is critical because the realm of motion is par excellence the realm of instruments, and no instrument can record/gauge anything in the realm of action ('ideas') except insofar as the subject-matter can be reduced to motion. Naturalist philosophers draw 'doctrinal sustenance from unrecognized effects of the pathetic fallacy as we have here extended it.'

positions.label: The incipient act is fundamentally ambiguous — substitute-for-act AND first-step-toward-act simultaneously
positions.claim: Burke's central extension of Richards. The realm of the incipient is the realm of symbolic action par excellence because symbolic action has the same ambiguous potentialities as overt action. This is the chapter's strongest single contribution to a phenomenology of intention and to any cross-pipeline crosswalk with Calleja PIM, Aristotelian phantasia, or Heideggerian pathē.

positions.label: Realism vs nominalism resolves on a single grammatical formula: members-of-group vs aggregate-of-individuals
positions.anchor: p.248 (Realist Family and Nominalist Aggregate subsection)
positions.claim: 'Realism treats individuals as members of a group, whereas nominalism treats groups as aggregates of individuals.' Realism fits clan-origin Greek democracy and Western feudal familial patterns; nominalism is 'anti-social' grammatically (obliterates consubstantiality, leaving 'world of individuals united only by monetary symbols and the deceptions of an idealistic rhetoric').

positions.label: Every ratio in Burke's pentad is reversible AND in potential-to-actual form, expanding the 10 ratios to 20
positions.anchor: p.262 (close of Further Remarks on Act and Potency subsection)
positions.claim: Members of any ratio pair are related as potential to actual. Scene-agent ratio situates in scene certain potentialities actualized in agent; agent-scene reverses. 'A ratio is a formula indicating a transition from one term to another' — the mediated differs from the immediate as translation from original. This generalizes the potency-actuality reciprocity from Aristotle to the entire pentadic apparatus.

positions.label: Aristotle's metaphysics is itself dramatist: pure act = end of motion = motivates as passive (the loved/desired)
positions.anchor: pp.230-231 + p.245 + p.253 + p.255 (Aristotle and Aquinas + Further Remarks subsections)
positions.claim: Aristotle's God as unmoved mover takes grammatical form of a passive (in being object of desire/eromenon); is conceived dramatistically as end-of-action; is paradoxically lyrical (perfect rest) rather than dramatic. This is the chapter's deepest justification for treating Aristotle's metaphysics — not just his poetics — as dramatist.

positions.label: All psychologies can be approached dramatistically as vocabularies of action and passion (including behaviorism)
positions.claim: Action-passion + actus-status + action-motion + potential are the four motivational pairs that organize any psychological vocabulary. Frustration/fixation/complex = passion; adjustment/normality = action; sublimation = transcendence; repression = new dialectic of reason. Behaviorism belongs here too via its concept of 'transference' (interpretation and classification of signs, capable of modification by linguistic means).

positions.label: Burke's appreciation of Aristotle is itself un-Aristotelian; the chapter is not arguing for any one traditional application of dramatist grammar
positions.anchor: p.252 (opening of Further Remarks on Act and Potency)
positions.claim: Methodological self-distancing: Burke's reading of Aristotle would not satisfy a Thomist; his remarks about Aquinas would not satisfy a Thomist. The chapter is a REVIEW of dialectical resources from the dramatist standpoint, not a manifesto for scholastic realism. This is essential for the dissertation: Burke's apparatus is recoverable WITHOUT inheriting the scholastic ontology.

tensions.label: Aristotle's dramatist metaphysics paradoxically produces a LYRICAL God
tensions.description: Aristotle's God as final cause of motion / unmoved mover is conceived dramatistically (as end-of-action), but pure act = perfect rest, which Burke explicitly classes as LYRIC (summation-of-action transcending overt action) not dramatic (pre-action). The chapter's deepest internal tension: a dramatist metaphysics requires a non-dramatic-because-perfectly-actualized telos. Tension is generative not destructive — it grounds the reversibility of pure act (final cause = efficient cause) and the egressus/regressus oxymoron.

tensions.label: The incipient act is fundamentally ambiguous and the ambiguity cannot be analytically resolved without losing the phenomenon
tensions.anchor: p.236 (Burke's extension of Richards) + p.243 (symbolic action realm)
tensions.description: An attitude/incipient-act is SIMULTANEOUSLY substitute-for-act AND first-step-toward-act, and any attempt to determine which is operative in a given case collapses the symbolic-action territory. This is the tension that makes the chapter the chief load-bearing site for dissertation crosswalk to game-user-motive analysis: the very ambiguity is the phenomenon, and any pipeline framework that requires resolution of the ambiguity will fail to track symbolic action.

tensions.label: Korzybski's delayed-action in the realm of motion must be the OPPOSITE of a delay
tensions.description: Burke's exposure of a paradox internal to Korzybski's semantics: from the standpoint of action, the consciousness-of-abstracting is a delay; but the physiological body that hosts this 'delay' must be unusually PROMPT in instantiating the particular nerve/muscle/endocrine configuration corresponding to arrest. The body during delay does not cease to exist; mental attitude of arrest must have its own bodily posture. There is at least as much neural motion in the hesitating body as in the unhesitating body. The tension exposes a more general one: action-motion vocabularies cannot be 'merged' without the merger inheriting the ambiguity rather than dissolving it.

tensions.label: Burke's appreciation of Aristotle is itself un-Aristotelian — the chapter REUSES scholastic-realist apparatus without endorsing scholastic ontology
tensions.description: Self-acknowledged methodological tension at the opening of Further Remarks. Burke is recovering dramatist resources from realism without committing to realism's metaphysical truth. The tension supplies the chapter's permission-structure for dissertation use: a game-studies theorist can deploy Burke's Act-operationalization without inheriting either Aristotelian hylomorphism or Thomist hierarchy.

tensions.label: The chapter's distinction between drama (PRE-act) and lyric (SUMMATION) cannot fully accommodate Hamlet, which is dramatically committed to being pre-act-that-amounts-to-no-act
tensions.description: Burke himself flags: Shakespeare in Hamlet nearly dissolves drama into pre-action-amounting-to-no-action, opposite to O'Neill's behaviorist dissolution. The drama/lyric distinction Burke has just established is, on his own admission, threatened from both poles by limit-cases. The Hamletic-strategy generalization to legislative committee-appointment is a graceful escape but does not fully resolve the genre-categorical strain.
